case_name: West v Canadian Direct Insurance Incorporated
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

West v. Canadian Direct Insurance
Incorporated,

2021 BCSC 740

Date: 20210414

Docket:
S154836

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Diane
Jane West

Plaintiff

And

Canadian Direct Insurance Incorporated, Don, Gail & Dillon (Tom)
Markley, Intact Insurance, City of Surrey-Risk Management, Westland Insurance –
(John Russell/Rohit Singh), Crawford & Company, Garnet Oliver

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Duncan

Oral Reasons for Judgment

The Plaintiff appearing on her own behalf:

D.J.
West

Counsel for the Defendants, Canadian
Direct Insurance Incorporated, Intact Insurance, Crawford & Company and
Garnet Oliver:

S.
Sidhu

Counsel for the Defendants, Westland
Insurance:

S.
Armstrong

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

April
7, 2021

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

April
14, 2021

[
1
]

There are two applications before the court, one
by Canadian Direct Insurance Incorporated (“CDI”), Intact Insurance, Crawford
and Company and Garnet Oliver (the “Intact defendants”) and one by Westland
Insurance, Rohit Singh and John Russell (the “Westland defendants”). Both
applications seek the same remedy: to strike the Amended Notice of Civil Claim
(the “ANOCC”) filed by the plaintiff Diane West on December 11, 2020 in its
entirety with no leave to amend.

[
2
]

This matter has an unusual history. On or about
May 29, 2014, a tree fell on or near the plaintiff’s property in Surrey,
resulting in damage. The plaintiff filed a notice of civil claim (“NOCC”)
alleging breach of contract against the Intact defendants, then doing business
as CDI. Crawford & Company and Garnet Oliver were not named in the original
NOCC.

[
3
]

The matter proceeded to trial in 2016 before
Madam Justice Russell. Ms. West acted for herself. Russell J. issued judgment
on October 17, 2016. The reasons are reported as
West v. Canadian Direct
Insurance
,
2016 BCSC 1903
, docket number S154836, the same action number
borne by the ANOCC.

[
4
]

Ms. West advanced claims of breach of contract
as well as claims for special and aggravated damages for bad faith insurance
practices and for surveillance and trespass to her house. Specifically, she
alleged that the defendant insurer surreptitiously entered her house to do
repairs in order to minimize the overall damage and used harmful construction
chemicals, poisoning her pets and polluting her water system. Ms. West also
sought to have her house replaced in its entirety.

[
5
]

Russell J. summarized the claims advanced at
trial:

[14]      In argument, [Ms. West] claimed
that the white van hit by the tree in the driveway, had shown much more damage
initially. In addition, she asserted that the VIN number of the van has been
removed, the pin striping that was on the van is now gone, and that either this
is a different van or the defendant has done some repair to raise the doors of
the van to minimize the crush damage caused by the tree.

[15]      She also alleged that the
defendant has done the following:  had her followed, stolen her original Policy
and substituted a different one for it, has hacked her computer to remove or
doctor photos of the damage she had suffered, has deleted her original Proof of
Loss, has deliberately lost supporting receipts, has removed correspondence from
her computer files, has interfered with her efforts to find counsel, and has
conspired with unnamed persons to cause harm to her health that resulted in a
hole to her macula, attempted to cause her death while she was in hospital
recovering from eye surgery, and subsequently corrupted her prescription eye
medication.

[16]      In argument, she alleged that at
least two of the defendant’s witnesses were not the persons of the same name
she had dealt with at her home but were impersonators.

[17]      She argued that the Canadian
Security Intelligence Service (“CSIS”) would be able to support her contention
that the Insurer had entered her house because CSIS has been watching it.
However, she advised the court that when she contacted CSIS to come to testify,
that agency advised its employees could not serve as witnesses due to security
issues and that most of their cases were in reference to terrorism.

[18]      She also stated that the insurer
had placed surveillance personnel on the house behind hers to spy on her and
that she knew this was so because these workers pretended to be roofers when
the house they were working on had been reroofed only 3 or 4 years ago.

[19]      As some of these allegations came
forward, I requested that the plaintiff provide me with a letter from her
doctor stating that the doctor found her capable of managing her day-to-day
affairs. In response, I received a very short statement signed by a doctor so
stating. That document is marked as Exhibit 72 in this proceeding.

[20]      On
receipt of that letter, the trial continued. However, I warned the plaintiff on
many occasions that there was no evidence of her allegations, they were not
properly pleaded and that the case would proceed on the breach of contract
allegation she made that the defendant had refused to indemnify her under the
Policy for damage to her property occasioned by the tree falling.

[
6
]

The plaintiff was largely unsuccessful at trial,
but was awarded damages for some of her collateral losses, such as the loss of
food in her refrigerator and freezer. She did not appeal the judgment.

[
7
]

In 2018, the defendant Westland Insurance Co.
Ltd., the legal name of the Westland defendant, issued a home insurance policy
to Ms. West. In December 2018, another tree fell on Ms. West’s property. She
made a claim to Westland for damage. Westland issued payment in June 2019 for
the estimated cost of repair, less the $1,000 deductible. Ms. West refused to
accept the payment. Instead, on December 11, 2020 Ms. West filed the ANOCC,
allegedly pursuant to an order of Russell J. on October 17, 2016, the date the
reasons for judgment were issued. The ANOCC bore the same docket number as the
claim adjudicated by Russell J.

[
8
]

Ms. West added the City of Surrey as a
defendant. She also added the Westland defendants as well as Crawford & Company
and Garnet Oliver. None of those entities were parties to the original action.

[
9
]

Ms. West appears to believe that Russell J.
ordered a stay of proceedings and placed Ms. West and her children in
protective custody so her claims could be investigated. She maintains she is
being hunted, that people come into her house and change documents on her
computer. She also maintains that people have come into her house to take her
bike and her kitchen appliances.

[
10
]

The ANOCC is 40 pages long. In cursive handwriting, it says “By
Order of Judge Russell October 17, 2016” on the front page. It starts out with
allegations about impersonators and a claim that the plaintiff’s house was to
be replaced and damages covered in the amount of $650,000, then segues to subjects
such as:

•

allegations that a neighbour enlisted the RCMP
to have her taken in for a mental health evaluation;

•

that actions by her home insurers have
contributed to her failing health;

•

allegations that the plaintiff had developed a
proposal for Translink concerning housing for the 2010 Olympics which fell
through because “malicious members” of the insurance claims could have
interfered with the proposal;

•

difficulties the plaintiff encountered during
exercise classes at a facility where the sons of the neighbour who allegedly
had her assessed for mental health issues worked;

•

criminal harassment;

•

criminal extortion where “even people at the
pool” were telling her to sell the house;

•

threats by the defendants to the plaintiff and
her family;

•

theft of items from her property;

•

impersonation of various officials by the
defendants;

•

manipulation of the medical system to put her in
danger; and

•

surveillance.

[
11
]

Ms. West claims damages in the amount of $1,500,000 for lost
contents as well as $146,000,000 for herself and her children; $146,000,000 for
the first responders who protected her and her family; and a variety of other
heads of relief.

The legal basis for the application

[
12
]

Both sets of defendants rely on Rule 9-5(1)(a) through (d) in
support of the application to strike the ANOCC in its entirety. They also rely
on Rule 6-2(7) in relation to the plaintiff’s effort to add parties who were
not part of the claim determined by Russell J.

[
13
]

Rule 9-5(1) states:

(1) At any stage of a proceeding, the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading,
petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses no
reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing
of the proceeding, or

(d) it is otherwise
an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
14
]

It must be “plain and obvious” that the pleading
discloses no reasonable cause of action for a successful application to strike
out a NOCC under Rule 9-5(1)(a):
R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,

2011 SCC 42
, [
Imperial Tobacco
], which stated the test as follows:

[17]      The parties agree on the test
applicable on a motion to strike for not disclosing a reasonable cause of action
under r. 19(24)(a) of the B.C. Supreme Court Rules [now R. 9-5(1)(a)]. This
Court has reiterated the test on many occasions. A claim will only be struck if
it is plain and obvious, assuming the facts pleaded to be true, that the
pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action:
Odhavji Estate v.
Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69
, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 263, at para.
15
;
Hunt v. Carey
Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, at p. 980. Another way of putting the
test is that the claim has no reasonable prospect of success. Where a
reasonable prospect of success exists, the matter should be allowed to proceed
to trial: see, generally,
Syl Apps Secure Treatment Centre v. B.D.
,
2007
SCC 38
, [2007] 3 S.C.R. 83;
Odhavji Estate
;
Hunt
;
Attorney
General of Canada v. Inuit Tapirisat of Canada
,
1980 CanLII 21 (SCC)
, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 735.

...

[22]      A motion to strike for failure to
disclose a reasonable cause of action proceeds on the basis that the facts
pleaded are true, unless they are manifestly incapable of being proven:
Operation
Dismantle Inc. v. The Queen
,
1985 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441, at p. 455. No evidence is
admissible on such a motion: r. 19(27) of the Supreme Court Rules (now r.
9-5(2) ... ). It is incumbent on the claimant to clearly plead the facts upon
which it relies in making its claim. A claimant is not entitled to rely on the
possibility that new facts may turn up as the case progresses. The claimant may
not be in a position to prove the facts pleaded at the time of the motion. It
may only hope to be able to prove them. But plead them it must. The facts
pleaded are the firm basis upon which the possibility of success of the claim
must be evaluated. If they are not pleaded, the exercise cannot be properly
conducted.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
15
]

In
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2015 BCSC 392
, Voith J.,
as he then was, summarized the test for striking pleadings under Rule 9-5(1).
After stating the test concerning Rule 9-5(1)(a), Voith J. said:

[58]      The test for striking a pleading
under R. 9-5(1)(b), on the basis that it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous
or vexatious, was recently summarized in
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC
1083
, where Fisher J. said:

[20]      Under Rule 9-5(1)(b), a pleading
is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s
cause of action, if it does not advance any claim known in law, where it is
obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it would serve no useful
purpose and would be a waste of the court’s time and public resources:
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No. 2160
(SC);
Skender v. Farley
,
2007 BCCA 629
. If a pleading is so confusing
that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, it may also be unnecessary,
frivolous or vexatious.

[59]      An “embarrassing” pleading, as
contemplated by R. 9-5(1)(c), is one that is so irrelevant that to allow it to
stand would involve useless expense and would also prejudice the trial of the
action by involving the parties in a dispute apart from the issues;
Keddie
v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (C.A.).

[60]      The abuse of process standard
under R. 9-5(1)(d) derives from a flexible doctrine. It allows the court to
prevent a claim from proceeding where to do so would violate principles of judicial
economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of
justice;
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at paras.

35-37
.

[61]      Though subsections (a)-(d) of R.
9-5(1) address different concerns and different wrongs, there is also some
overlap between these subsections. Thus, for example, a pleading that discloses
no cause of action, contrary to R. 9-5(1)(a), can also be unnecessary,
frivolous or vexatious within the meaning of  R. 9-5(1)(b); see e.g.
Virk v.
Brar
,
2012 BCSC 1004
at paras.
69-70
.

[62]      A
pleading can be embarrassing if it does not state the real issue in an
intelligible form. It can also be embarrassing if it is prolix, includes
irrelevant facts, argument or evidence. It can be prejudicial if it is designed
to or has the effect of confusing the defendant, making it difficult, if not
impossible, to answer;
Virk
at para.
75
.

[
16
]

In addition, bringing an action to determine an issue that has
already been adjudicated constitutes a vexatious proceeding:
Skender v.
Farley
,
2007 BCCA 629
at para.
64
.

[
17
]

Upon a careful review of the ANOCC, it is impossible to determine
whether the plaintiff has articulated any new causes of action. The ANOCC is
utterly nonsensical and illogical.

[
18
]

Even if one could extract discernible new causes of action, they
cannot proceed under the guise of an ANOCC because the cause of action which
was the subject of original claim has been conclusively determined. There is no
stay or any other mechanism at law which could permit Ms. West to file new allegations
in this manner. The original NOCC was conclusively dealt with by Russell J. in
her reasons for judgment. It is spent.

[
19
]

In light of my conclusion that the plaintiff’s ANOCC is procedurally
a nullity, it is not necessary to determine the defendants’ alternate
application for relief based on the plaintiff’s failure to properly add
Crawford & Company, Garnet Oliver and the Westland defendants. I agree,
however, that to the extent the plaintiff has tried to add parties, she has
failed to do so properly under Rule 6-2(7). In any event, that Rule does not
apply after judgment:
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce v. Garneau
,

1986 CanLII 992 (BC SC)
, [1986] B.C.J. No. 2362 at paras.
17-18
.

[
20
]

The ANOCC is struck in its entirety, with no leave to amend it. This
does not prevent Ms. West from filing a fresh NOCC alleging a cause of action
other than the one conclusively determined by Russell J. Ms. West may have some
sort of claim against the Westland defendants in relation to her insurance
coverage under the policy they issued to her. Counsel for the Westland
defendants suggested that some guidance or restrictions be placed on Ms. West’s
ability to file a new NOCC, but Ms. West has not been declared a vexatious
litigant and there is no authority to pre-emptively circumscribe an individual’s
right to file a NOCC.

[
21
]

The applicants are entitled to costs at Scale B, payable forthwith.

“Duncan
J.”
